conflicts: His own 1991 narration says 'for the duration of my employment at S4 I was paid by the United States Navy'. The W-2 form as others describe it names a 'Department of Naval Intelligence', which is not an entity that exists; the Office of Naval Intelligence sits inside the Department of the Navy. The two statements are not the same statement, and the board carries the discrepancy rather than resolving it, because the form itself was not opened.

The Teller anecdote has a date problem. His 1991 narration puts the Los Alamos Monitor jet-car story and Edward Teller's Los Alamos speech on the same day. Tom Mahood's 2018 retrospective puts the Monitor article on 27 June 1982 and Teller's lecture on the following day. The newspaper's own date is fixed, so both cannot be right. The anecdote survives as 'within a day' and is carried as such.

The sentence is described differently by two reliable routes. The Las Vegas Review-Journal of 21 August 1990 reports probation with 150 hours of community service and psychotherapy. Douglas Dean Johnson, working from the court file, describes a three-year suspended sentence with probation, completed. These are compatible readings of one disposition but they are not the same wording, and no session has reconciled them against the judgment of conviction itself.

label: Robert "Bob" Lazar
narrative: Bob Lazar is the origin point of the best-known claim in the field and, on the opened record, he is a contract electronics technician rather than the physicist the claim requires. In 1982 he worked at Los Alamos, and the Los Alamos Monitor of 27 June 1982 described him on its front page as 'a physicist at the Los Alamos Meson Physics Facility'. That description is the strongest documentary thread in his favour and it carries its own qualification: the Los Alamos telephone directory page that also lists his name states on its face that it covers Department of Energy employees and the outside contractor Kirk-Mayer, and a Los Alamos colleague interviewed on tape in 1996 said Lazar 'was a contractor' under Kirk Mayer. In 1989 he told KLAS-TV in Las Vegas, first silhouetted under the pseudonym 'Dennis' and then under his own name, that between December 1988 and April 1989 he had worked at a facility called S-4, about fifteen miles south of Groom Lake, back-engineering the propulsion of nine disc-shaped craft fuelled by a stable isotope of element 115. In 1991 he fixed that account in datable form by narrating it himself on a forty-minute videotape produced with his friend Gene Huff. The credential half of his account has been checked by named people and does not survive: no institutional record of the MIT or Caltech degrees exists, and the professor he named as a Caltech instructor turned out to teach at Pierce Junior College, where Lazar had taken at least one of his classes. The credential question is Tier 1 rather than gossip because Lazar's own reported education, listing a 1978 Pacifica University BS alongside the MIT and Caltech degrees, is printed in his Pre-Sentence Report of 27 July 1990, a Clark County court document produced after he pleaded guilty to felony pandering. What makes him a node is proximity to the claim, not credibility: no clearance is documented anywhere in the opened record, no office, and no physical trace of anything he describes.
